This page holds the exercise of the course, Tasks 1 to 5, on a copy of R that runs inside the browser, with the data already in place and the same helper functions as the downloadable workspace. The slides of the live decks run the same cells, and this page is the fallback when a deck does not load. The short format is worked in its deck, and the day and independent formats in the downloadable workspace, which holds the same tasks for anyone who has installed R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.). Nothing done in a deck, on this page or in the workspace is wasted, since all three fit the same models to the same data and give the same numbers.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## While the R engine loads

The R engine downloads into your browser the first time you open this page (a minute or so, longer on a slow connection). Read Task 1 while it loads. You will know that it is ready when the first code cell switches from a loading spinner to a "Run Code" button.

Keep this tab open. Your work stays in this page until you refresh it – there is nothing to install, nothing to save to disk, and no account needed.
:::

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true
#| output: false
# Shared setup – this runs automatically once the engine is ready. It loads
# the Housing data into your browser session as `housing`, one row per
# email, the object from which the cells below work. The file arrives at

.data_dir <- "data"
housing <- utils::read.csv("data/housing_emails.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))
```

{{< include _includes/_lab-helpers.qmd >}}

Five analysts reanalysed a claim of the Housing case study [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] for the robustness study of SCORE [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]; you are analyst no. 6. The claim is that "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts", in the words of the original authors (OAs) as the SCORE programme selected them. The [background page](background.qmd) presents the original study, the robustness study and the five reanalyses.

The five tasks take you from a setup check to two marks on the live class chart, one submitted while you explore the menu in Task 4 and one that you declare in your preregistration in Task 5 before running it. The pages of your format say which tasks it covers, and whether it sends anything to the class chart. Every fit on this page is live: the estimator of the course runs in your browser, on the same file and with the same code as in the workspace.

## Task 1 – The setup check {#task-1-setup}

The aim of this task is only to reach the point where a line of R runs and the data are in front of you. Press **Run Code** on the cell below. If it prints the three lines that it should, you are set up and everything else on this page will work.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# The setup check. It uses only what the page preloads, so if this runs, the
# rest of the lab runs.
writeLines(c(
  paste("R is running in your browser:", R.version.string),
  sprintf("The emails are loaded: %d rows", nrow(housing)),
  sprintf("The estimator reproduces the reference specification: %.2f percentage points",
          fit_spec(housing)$b_pp)))
```

You should see **1,014 rows** and **−19.97 percentage points** on the last line. If any of that is missing, reload the page and wait for the engine to finish downloading before pressing Run Code again. If it still fails, say **STUCK** in the chat.

## Warm-up – the three Rs {#warm-up}

The warm-up settles the vocabulary before you touch any data. Three of the four scenarios below describe one of our three Rs – reproducibility, robustness, replicability – and the fourth describes something else. Read all four, then label each one in the code cell.

***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer runs the Stata `.do` file of the OAs on their public data file and gets a coefficient for Hispanic names that differs from the one printed in the paper, because the public file holds the size, poverty and ethnic composition of each community in thirds rather than as the census values. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though the numbers do not match.

***Scenario 2:*** An analyst takes the same public file, re-implements the analysis in R instead of Stata, and also counts the five replies that carry no greeting code as replies without a greeting. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_?

***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team emails 3,050 public housing authorities with four new names and finds no difference in how often the replies greet the sender by name. Their conclusion is that the original finding has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_.

***Scenario 4:*** Another researcher asks whether the same bias appears when people telephone school districts rather than email housing authorities, codes recorded voice messages instead of written replies, and finds the same pattern. The researcher concludes that the original finding \_\_\_\_\_\_ to another service and another medium.

Fill in the gaps in the code cell below and run it to print your answers back.

```{webr}
#| exercise: vocab
#| code-overflow: wrap
writeLines(c(
  "Scenario 1: This is an example of ______.",
  "Scenario 2: Is this a case of ______ or ______?",
  "Scenario 3: The original finding has failed to ______.",
  "Scenario 4: The original finding ______ to another service and another medium."
))
```

:::: {.solution exercise="vocab"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Answers

1.  **reproducibility** – rerunning the code of the OAs on their data. The numbers differ, but the activity is still reproduction, and the difference has a documented cause: the blinded file.
2.  a grey area. Re-implementing on the same data in different software is still **reproducibility**, but recoding the uncoded replies is an analytic choice, which makes it a test of **robustness**.
3.  **replicability** – the same question asked of independent new data.
4.  **generalises** (generalisability) – the odd one out, with a new population, new data and a new measure at once.
:::
::::

## Task 2 – The data {#task-2-data}

The **Housing data** (`housing_emails.csv`) are already loaded for you as `housing`, one row per email. The file is built from the public file of the OAs on Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU, released under CC0), with plainer column names; the downloadable workspace contains the same file. Run the cell below to count what came back. Edit it freely – this is your environment.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# How many emails, and what came back?
housing |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails    = n(),
                           bounced   = sum(is.na(reply)),
                           delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)),
                           replies   = sum(reply %in% 1),
                           coded     = sum(!is.na(named)))
```

You should find **1,014 emails** (the paper reports 1,017, three more than the public file holds), of which **23 bounced** and never reached an official, **991 delivered**, **563 replies**, and **558 replies with a greeting code**. The column `reply` is 1 for a reply, 0 for none and missing for a bounced email. `named` is 1 when a reply greeted the sender by name, 0 when it did not, and missing for every email without a reply and for the five replies that carry no greeting code. The [codebook](data/housing_emails_codebook.md) describes every column.

Now the replies and the greetings by the group of the name:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(delivered   = n(),
                           replies     = sum(reply == 1),
                           coded       = sum(!is.na(named)),
                           greeted     = sum(named %in% 1),
                           greeted_pct = round(100 * sum(named %in% 1) / sum(!is.na(named)), 1),
                           by = "group")
```

Tables print in this lab as plain text, as they would in the console of your IDE. To read one as a formatted table, add `|> gt::gt()` to the end of the cell and run it again, or, for the output of `datawizard::data_summary()`, `datawizard::data_tabulate()` and `parameters::model_parameters()`, add `|> datawizard::print_html()` or `|> parameters::print_html()`, which also round the numbers. In your own IDE and in the report of the workspace, `tinytable::tt()` does this job, but it cannot display its tables on this page.

Then the share greeted by name for each of the six names. This cell works out the shares and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# The share greeted by name for each of the six names, from the lowest
greeted <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(greeted_pct = 100 * mean(named), by = c("group", "name")) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("greeted_pct") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(group = factor(group, levels = c("white", "black", "hispanic"),
                                         labels = c("white", "Black", "Hispanic")))
```

The next cell draws them, a bar for each name with its share at the end.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
# The shares drawn with tinyplot (McDermott, Arel-Bundock and Zeileis; CRAN,
# doi:10.32614/CRAN.package.tinyplot)
tinyplot::tinyplot(greeted_pct ~ name | group, data = greeted,
                   type = tinyplot::type_barplot(xlevels = greeted$name, width = 0.7, drop.zeros = TRUE), flip = TRUE,
                   palette = c("grey60", "#4a78ab", "#8b1538"), fill = "by",
                   legend = list("right!", title = "Names meant to indicate"),
                   xlab = NA, ylab = "Replies that greeted the sender by name (%)",
                   ylim = c(0, 72), theme = "minimal")
# the share at the end of each bar
tinyplot::tinyplot(x = seq_len(nrow(greeted)), y = greeted$greeted_pct, flip = TRUE,
                   type = tinyplot::type_text(labels = sprintf("%.1f%%", greeted$greeted_pct), pos = 4),
                   cex = 0.9, add = TRUE)
```

The replies to white names greeted the sender by name in 61.1% of cases, those to Hispanic names in 41.2%: a gap of about 20 points, the size of the published estimate. Black names fall in between, at 56.1%, and of the six names Santiago received the fewest greetings by name.

## Task 2, continued – The estimand and the graph {#task-2-estimand-and-graph}

Before fitting anything, say what you are trying to estimate, in words. A template that you can adapt:

> The **unit-specific quantity** is, for each housing authority, the difference between whether it would come back with a reply that greets the sender by name to an email signed with a Hispanic name and to the same email signed with a white name. The **target population** is the public housing authorities that received an email.

There is a catch in that sentence. An authority whose official would not reply to one of the names has no greeting to compare. The comparison can then count every delivered email, a missing reply counting as no greeting, or count the replies only, which compares the authorities that replied to Hispanic names with those that replied to white names. These need not be the same authorities.

A causal graph makes the catch visible. A graph of this kind is a diagram of what causes what: variables are nodes, arrows run from cause to effect, and the rules for reading the graph say which paths between the name and the greeting are open, given what the comparison conditions on. The graph below is written in ordinary R, one arrow per string, each written the way it is drawn: `"name -> reply"` is the arrow from the name to the reply. The name can affect whether the official replies, and only a reply can greet the sender by name. Something about the official that nobody recorded (workload, habits of courtesy, attitudes) affects both whether they reply and how they greet, and so does the community of the housing authority. One arrow is switched off with a `#`: the arrow from the name to the greeting, which is the effect on tone that the claim is about.

{{< include _includes/_lab-graph.qmd >}}

`make_dag()`, `adjustmentSets()`, `paths()` and `plot_dag()` are already available on this page, so you can go straight to the graph. In the downloadable workspace the two questions go to `dagitty`, the R package for causal graphs, which cannot run on this page. Here `adjustmentSets()` and `paths()` print the answers that dagitty gives, read from a table that the course computed with dagitty for the graph of the cell below, with and without the arrow of the claim ([codebook](data/dag_answers_codebook.md)). Any other graph gets a pointer to the workspace.

Now build the graph and put two questions to it. The cell below builds the graph from its arrows and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_dag <- make_dag(
  # The name can affect whether the official replies at all.
  "name -> reply",
  # Only a reply can greet the sender by name.
  "reply -> greeting",
  # The official, whom nobody observed, affects both the reply and the greeting.
  "official -> reply",
  "official -> greeting",
  # So does the community of the housing authority, held in thirds in the data.
  "community -> reply",
  "community -> greeting",

  # The effect on tone that the claim is about: take the # off if you believe it.
  # "name -> greeting",

  exposure = "name", outcome = "greeting", latent = "official"
)
```

The first question is what has to be adjusted for when the comparison counts every delivered email:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
adjustmentSets(my_dag)
```

The second is which paths from the name to the greeting are open once the comparison is made among replies only, which is what `Z = "reply"` asks: it conditions on the reply.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
paths(my_dag, Z = "reply")
```

The last cell draws the graph.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_dag(my_dag)
```

`adjustmentSets()` returns `{}`, the empty set: nothing has to be adjusted for, because nothing points into the name. The names were assigned at random, so no common cause of the name and the greeting can exist. Conditioning on the reply changes the picture. The path through the reply closes, but two paths open, one through the community and one through the official, because the reply is a common effect of the name and of each of them (a collider), and comparing replies only conditions on it. This is the problem of conditioning on a consequence of the treatment, which @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias sets out for audit experiments.

Now take the `#` off the arrow `"name -> greeting"` in the cell that builds the graph, and run that cell and the three after it again. Then run the cell below, which also adjusts for the community. Answer three questions for your own notes: why the adjustment set stays empty; which paths stay open among replies once the community is adjusted for, and what that means for a gap among replies; and which emails keep the comparison randomised.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
paths(my_dag, Z = c("reply", "community"))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers

1.  The set stays `{}` because nothing points into the name, whatever arrows leave it: the names were randomised.
2.  The direct path and the path through the official stay open. A gap among replies mixes the effect of the name on tone with differences between the officials who reply to each name, and adjusting for the community cannot remove the second, because the official is unobserved.
3.  Every delivered email, a missing reply counting as no greeting. That comparison estimates the effect of the name on receiving a greeting by name at all, which mixes the decision to reply with the tone of the reply.

The difference between the two comparisons is the decision on which emails are counted, the second argument of `try_spec()` in Task 4, and whatever you conclude here belongs in field 4 of your preregistration in Task 5.
:::

## Task 3 – The reproduction {#task-3-reproduction}

This is the **reproducibility** check. Five analysts reanalysed the claim for the robustness study, each with code of their own, and the robustness study recorded a test statistic for four of them. Choose one of the five and reproduce the analysis from the public file of the OAs, `housing_original.csv`, which keeps their column names. `Response_Dichotomous` is 1 for a reply, 0 for none and empty for a bounced email. `ProperName` is the greeting by name, empty for every email that has no reply with a greeting code. `TreatmentGroup` holds the group and the sex of the name (`"Hispanic male"`, `"white female"` and so on).

| Analyst | What the analysis compared | Emails counted | Test | Recorded in the robustness study |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [8PTRZ](#task-3-8ptrz) | Hispanic names against all other names | the 558 replies with a greeting code | chi-square test of a 2 × 2 table | $\chi^2$ = 14.265 |
| [UYV3F](#task-3-uyv3f) | Hispanic against white names | the 362 coded replies to those names | logistic regression without covariates | z = −3.771 |
| [EWFMI](#task-3-ewfmi) | the three groups, with Hispanic names as the base | the 549 coded replies that carry a poverty third | logistic regression with the sex of the name, the poverty third and the hard-to-find address | z = 3.645 |
| [25N5D](#task-3-25n5d) | Hispanic against white names | the 665 delivered emails to those names, a missing reply counted as no greeting | two-proportion test | $\chi^2$ = 13.683 |
| [P9W8Y](#task-3-p9w8y) | the three groups | the 558 replies with a greeting code | likelihood-ratio test of a logistic regression | none |

Each analyst has a few cells of their own below, one step each, to be run in order. One of the cells of each analyst is an exercise: replace the blank (`______`) with the missing code, then press "Run Code". A hint and the solution sit under that cell. When you have your value, type the analyst and the value into the chat, for example `UYV3F z = -3.771`, hold it, and send it on the facilitator's word. The course computes the same five refits in its own pipeline, with the same functions, and the four recorded statistics all come out exactly ([`analysts5.csv`](data/analysts5_codebook.md)). For P9W8Y the robustness study recorded no statistic, so its analysis can be run again but there is nothing on record to match it against.

Whichever analyst you choose, run the cell below first. It reads the public file of the OAs as `original`, the object from which every later cell of this task works, and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
original <- utils::read.csv("data/housing_original.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))
```

### 8PTRZ – the test of a table {#task-3-8ptrz}

Analyst 8PTRZ compared Hispanic names with all other names, white and Black together, among the 558 replies that carry a greeting code, with a chi-square test of the 2 × 2 table. The robustness study recorded $\chi^2$ = 14.265.

```{webr}
#| exercise: repro-8ptrz
#| envir: global
# keep the replies that carry a greeting code, and mark the Hispanic names
coded_replies <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(______)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))
```

:::: {.hint exercise="repro-8ptrz"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the replies with a greeting code

`ProperName` is empty for every email without a reply, for the bounced emails and for the five replies without a greeting code, so keeping the rows in which it is not missing leaves the 558 coded replies.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="repro-8ptrz"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
coded_replies <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))
```
:::
::::

Then run the next two cells in order. The first makes the table and prints it, and the second tests it.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the 2 x 2 table: Hispanic or other name, by greeting
tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded_replies)
tab_8ptrz
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the chi-square test of the table
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)
```

You should get `X-squared = 14.265, df = 1`, the value on record for 8PTRZ.

### UYV3F – a logistic regression {#task-3-uyv3f}

Analyst UYV3F compared Hispanic with white names only, among the 362 coded replies to those names, with a logistic regression of the greeting on the name and no covariates. The robustness study recorded z = −3.771, the z of the coefficient of the Hispanic names.

The first cell keeps the rows of the analysis and prints nothing. The second, the exercise, fits the model.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the coded replies to Hispanic and white names, with the Hispanic names marked
replies_uyv3f <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName) & !grepl("^black", TreatmentGroup)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: repro-uyv3f
#| envir: global
# the logistic regression of the greeting on the name
m_uyv3f <- glm(ProperName ~ hispanic_name, family = ______(), data = replies_uyv3f)
nobs(m_uyv3f)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="repro-uyv3f"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the family of the model

A logistic regression is a generalised linear model of a 0/1 outcome with the family that R calls `binomial`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="repro-uyv3f"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
m_uyv3f <- glm(ProperName ~ hispanic_name, family = binomial(), data = replies_uyv3f)
nobs(m_uyv3f)
```
:::
::::

The last cell prints the coefficients.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the coefficients, with the z of each
print(parameters::model_parameters(m_uyv3f, ci_method = "wald"), digits = 3)
```

The row of the Hispanic names gives z = −3.771 on 362 replies, the value on record for UYV3F.

### EWFMI – a model of three groups {#task-3-ewfmi}

Analyst EWFMI fitted a logistic regression of the greeting on all three groups of names, with the Hispanic names as the base group, the sex of the name, the poverty third of the community entered as a number, and the hard-to-find address, in Stata. The 9 coded replies from communities without a poverty third drop out, which leaves 549. The robustness study recorded z = 3.645, the z of the white names against the Hispanic names.

```{webr}
#| exercise: repro-ewfmi
#| envir: global
# the coded replies, with TreatmentGroup split into the group and the sex of the name
replies_ewfmi <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_separate(select = "TreatmentGroup", new_columns = c("ethnicity", "name_sex"),
                            separator = " ", append = TRUE) |>
  # the first level of a factor is the base group of the model
  datawizard::data_modify(ethnicity = factor(ethnicity, levels = c("______", "black", "white")))
```

:::: {.hint exercise="repro-ewfmi"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the base group

The analyst compared the other groups with the Hispanic names, so `"Hispanic"` comes first among the levels, spelled as in `TreatmentGroup`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="repro-ewfmi"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
replies_ewfmi <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_separate(select = "TreatmentGroup", new_columns = c("ethnicity", "name_sex"),
                            separator = " ", append = TRUE) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(ethnicity = factor(ethnicity, levels = c("Hispanic", "black", "white")))
```
:::
::::

Then fit the model of EWFMI in the next cell, and print its coefficients in the one after it.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the model of EWFMI; a reply without a poverty third drops out
m_ewfmi <- glm(ProperName ~ ethnicity + name_sex + poverty_pop_third + HardEmail,
               family = binomial(), data = replies_ewfmi)
nobs(m_ewfmi)
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
print(parameters::model_parameters(m_ewfmi, ci_method = "wald"), digits = 3)
```

The row `ethnicity [white]` gives z = 3.645 on 549 replies, the value on record for EWFMI.

### 25N5D – every delivered email {#task-3-25n5d}

Analyst 25N5D compared Hispanic with white names among every email that was delivered, counting an email without a reply as one without a greeting, with the two-proportion test of R, `prop.test()`. The five replies without a greeting code stay in the denominators and count as no greeting. The robustness study recorded $\chi^2$ = 13.683 on 665 emails.

```{webr}
#| exercise: repro-25n5d
#| envir: global
# the delivered emails to Hispanic and white names; a bounced email has no reply status
emails_25n5d <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(______) & !grepl("^black", TreatmentGroup)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup),
                          greeted = Response_Dichotomous == 1 & ProperName %in% 1)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="repro-25n5d"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the delivered emails

`Response_Dichotomous` is empty for the 23 emails that bounced, so keeping the rows in which it is not missing keeps every delivered email.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="repro-25n5d"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
emails_25n5d <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(Response_Dichotomous) & !grepl("^black", TreatmentGroup)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup),
                          greeted = Response_Dichotomous == 1 & ProperName %in% 1)
```
:::
::::

Then run the next two cells in order. The first counts the greetings and the emails for each group of names, and the second tests the two proportions.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the greetings by name and the emails, for each group of names
counts_25n5d <- datawizard::data_summary(emails_25n5d, greetings = sum(greeted), emails = n(),
                                         by = "hispanic_name")
counts_25n5d
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the test of the two proportions
prop.test(counts_25n5d$greetings, counts_25n5d$emails)
```

You should get `X-squared = 13.683, df = 1` on 308 + 357 = 665 emails, the value on record for 25N5D.

### P9W8Y – a test of three groups {#task-3-p9w8y}

Analyst P9W8Y fitted a logistic regression of the greeting on the three groups of names among the 558 coded replies and tested whether the three differ at all, with a likelihood-ratio test of the model against a model without the groups. The robustness study recorded no statistic for this analysis, so the rerun cannot be matched against the record. The report that the analyst filed for Task 2 gives $\chi^2$ = 15.951 on 2 degrees of freedom in its text, and the rerun gives the same value. The verdict of "no evidence" in Task 1 came from another model, with an interaction between the group and the sex of the name, whose test of the groups compared the three female names only under the default coding of R.

The first cell keeps the coded replies and prints nothing, the second fits the model, and the third, the exercise, tests it.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the coded replies, with the group of the name as a factor
replies_p9w8y <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_separate(select = "TreatmentGroup", new_columns = c("ethnicity", "name_sex"),
                            separator = " ", append = TRUE) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(ethnicity = factor(ethnicity, levels = c("white", "black", "Hispanic")))
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# the model of the three groups
m_p9w8y <- glm(ProperName ~ ethnicity, family = binomial(), data = replies_p9w8y)
nobs(m_p9w8y)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: repro-p9w8y
#| envir: global
# the likelihood-ratio test against the same model without the groups
anova(update(m_p9w8y, . ~ 1), m_p9w8y, test = "______")
```

:::: {.hint exercise="repro-p9w8y"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the test

`anova()` compares two nested models fitted to the same rows; a likelihood-ratio test is asked for with `test = "LRT"`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="repro-p9w8y"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
anova(update(m_p9w8y, . ~ 1), m_p9w8y, test = "LRT")
```

The column `Deviance` gives 15.951 on 2 degrees of freedom for 558 replies. The record of the robustness study holds no value to compare it with.
:::
::::

### Defaults and codings {#task-3-defaults}

Now find out why your number is exactly that number. For a 2 × 2 table, `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` both apply the continuity correction of Yates unless they are told otherwise: it shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by 0.5 before squaring, a remedy designed for small tables. Neither 8PTRZ nor 25N5D asked for the correction. The defaults of the two functions applied it, and the recorded values are the corrected ones. The cells below run both tests without the correction, on the file read at the start of this task. The first three redo the comparison of 8PTRZ, and only the third, the test, prints anything.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# 8PTRZ: the replies with a greeting code, Hispanic against all other names
coded_replies <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded_replies)
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)
```

The last two count the delivered emails of 25N5D and test the two proportions.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# 25N5D: the delivered emails, Hispanic against white names
counts_25n5d <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(Response_Dichotomous) & !grepl("^black", TreatmentGroup)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup),
                          greeted = Response_Dichotomous == 1 & ProperName %in% 1) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(greetings = sum(greeted), emails = n(), by = "hispanic_name")
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
prop.test(counts_25n5d$greetings, counts_25n5d$emails, correct = FALSE)
```

Without the correction the two statistics are 14.95 and 14.33. Neither changes the conclusion, but only the corrected values match the record, and the description "a chi-square test" fits both. The coding of the data matters in the same way. The z of EWFMI is positive and the z of UYV3F negative, although both describe Hispanic names greeted by name less often, because EWFMI took the Hispanic names as the base group, so that the coefficient compares white names with Hispanic names. A reproduction needs the code, or at least every default and every coding on which the code relied.

The scripts that the analysts submitted are on the OSF, in the component of the robustness study for the paper ([osf.io/38rsh](https://osf.io/38rsh/)), one sub-component for each analyst: 8PTRZ [osf.io/j8wvh](https://osf.io/j8wvh/), UYV3F [osf.io/3672s](https://osf.io/3672s/) (a review document only), EWFMI [osf.io/jhvca](https://osf.io/jhvca/), 25N5D [osf.io/v8zah](https://osf.io/v8zah/) and P9W8Y [osf.io/pzwbm](https://osf.io/pzwbm/).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reproduction and the five analysts

You reproduced the value of the analyst whom you chose, and so did everyone else who chose the same analyst, because everyone ran the same code on the same file. This is why reproducibility is the cheapest of the three Rs to establish.

The five analysts of the robustness study each wrote their own code for this claim. Three concluded that the results were evidence for the claim and two that they were evidence neither for nor against it, although the four statistics recorded in the robustness study all come from gaps in the same direction. Part of the difference lies in the questions that each analyst chose to answer (which names to compare, which emails to count), and part in what each analyst took to count as evidence: one of the two who answered 'neither' found the gap but judged it substantially smaller than the published one. The [background page](background.qmd) sets out what each analyst chose.
:::

## Task 4 – The menu {#task-4-menu}

This task is **exploratory**. You try several specifications, look at what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. Nothing in this task is preregistered; the preregistration comes in Task 5.

`try_spec()` takes one argument per decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), and every argument defaults to the reference specification, the raw gap of the paper: Hispanic against white names, among the replies, the five uncoded replies left out, a difference in proportions without covariates. So changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays as it was. Every call is a live fit in your browser.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Nothing changed – the reference specification.
try_spec()
```

The printout gives the shares greeted by name in the two groups, the difference in percentage points with its 95% interval, the test of the model (a *t* with HC2 standard errors for the linear model, the *z* of the logit coefficient for the logit), the number of emails analysed, the partial *r* by the conversion rule of the robustness study, the class of the result, and its place among the 64 specifications on the curve of the claim.

Each of the five cells below changes a single decision. The first two change the question that is being asked of the data, the third changes how the outcome is measured, and the last two change only how the same question is estimated. Run the five in order and compare the results.

The first changes the comparison group.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(comparison = "nonhispanic")  # Hispanic names against white and Black names together
```

The second changes which emails are counted.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(population = "all")  # every delivered email, no reply counted as no greeting
```

The third changes how the replies without a greeting code are counted.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(uncoded = "not_named")  # the five uncoded replies counted as no greeting
```

The fourth changes the model.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(model = "logit")  # the model of the paper, as an average marginal effect
```

The fifth changes the adjustment.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(adjust = "place_ethnic")  # the covariates of the original model, in thirds
```

The menu holds more options than the curve, which keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way. Every other option is still an argument of `try_spec()`, so trying one is part of the exercise. The helper refuses it, gives the reason why it is not on the curve and names the page of the course that teaches it, and the [decision map](menu.qmd#map) sets out every decision and its options on one page. Run the cell, then edit it to try others, such as `outcome = "reply"`, `names = "male"`, `comparison = "black"`, `adjust = "acs_continuous"` or `inference = "one_tailed"`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# An option that is not on the curve: the helper refuses it and says why.
try_spec(model = "three_group")
```

Then try your own combinations. The full set of arguments, each with the reference specification as its default and the options of the menu in the comment beside it:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(
  # the five decisions on which the curve keeps more than one option
  comparison = "white",      # white | nonhispanic          off the curve: black
  population = "replies",    # replies | all
  uncoded    = "drop",       # drop | not_named
  model      = "lpm",        # lpm | logit                  off the curve: three_group
  adjust     = "none",       # none | email | place | place_ethnic
                             #                              off the curve: name_sex | acs_continuous
  # the six decisions that are fixed on the curve
  outcome    = "named",      # named                        off the curve: reply | reply24
  names      = "both",       # both                         off the curve: male | female
  officials  = "any",        # any                          off the curve: hispanic
  bounced    = "exclude",    # exclude                      off the curve: no_reply
  inference  = "model",      # model                        off the curve: randomisation | chisq | one_tailed
  scale      = "pp"          # pp                           off the curve: odds_ratio | r
)
```

Everything you try is logged. Print the log to view the small multiverse that you have just built. It shows only the decisions that you varied, so the differences are easy to read:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_experiments()
```

When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so that it is the most recent, and submit it. It appears on the live [class chart]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) as an open circle, labelled **exploratory**, and marked with the tag that the cell prints, such as `amber-otter-42`. The tag is how you find your own marks on the chart, and your declared result in Task 5 carries the same one. To choose your own, write `submit_exploration(nickname = "...")` with a nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
submit_exploration()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exploratory and declared

Because you chose this specification after finding out what several specifications do, it lacks the guarantee that comes with a choice declared in a preregistration before its result is known: no one can rule out that it was chosen *because* of its result. This is something that we almost never know about published papers, unless their analysis was preregistered and every departure from the preregistration documented. In this course exploration is a natural step, and you also practise preregistering the analysis that you choose, so you submit twice, once here and once in Task 5.
:::

## Task 5 – The preregistration {#task-5-preregistration}

Preregistration means setting out your choice in a plan **before** you know what it does, which stops you from quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. On this page the plan is the preregistration cell below, and it binds mechanically as well: the session remembers the choices that you declare in that cell, and `run_spec()` and `report_result()` read them from there.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## A shortened preregistration

*Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part that AsPredicted leaves out.*
:::

Make one choice on each decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), complete the dotted lines, then run the cell. The five decisions about the question fix what you are asking, the two measurement decisions fix how the outcome is counted, and the four decisions about the model fix how the answer is reached. The curve of 64 specifications keeps two or more options on five of these decisions and a single option on the other six.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: housing_emails.csv (1,014 emails, public,
#    CC0); I know that the reference specification gives -19.97 points, and
#    what my exploration in Task 4 showed.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each decision. An option that is
#    not on the curve of 64 stops prereg() with the reason why.

# The question (each of these changes what is being estimated)
my_outcome    <- "named"     # named   (greeted by name, the outcome of the claim)
my_comparison <- "white"     # white | nonhispanic   (white names, or white and Black names)
my_population <- "replies"   # replies | all   (replies only, or every delivered email)
my_names      <- "both"      # both   (male and female names pooled)
my_officials  <- "any"       # any    (replies from every official)

# Measurement (the same question, put to the data differently)
my_uncoded    <- "drop"      # drop | not_named   (the five replies without a greeting code)
my_bounced    <- "exclude"   # exclude   (the 23 emails that never arrived)

# The model (the same question and measures, another fit)
my_model      <- "lpm"       # lpm | logit   (difference in proportions, or logistic regression)
my_adjust     <- "none"      # none | email | place | place_ethnic
my_inference  <- "model"     # model   (HC2 t test, or the z test of the logit)
my_scale      <- "pp"        # pp   (percentage points)

# 4. Why this specification answers the claim, in one sentence grounded in
#    the causal graph of Task 2: .............................................
# 5. Supported if the estimate is below zero with p < .05 under the test of
#    the model; undermined if it is not significant or above zero. I will
#    report what I get.
```

Then run the cell below, which reads your choices. An option that is not on the curve stops `prereg()` with the reason why, as it stops `try_spec()`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_spec <- prereg()   # checks every choice, prints your preregistration and keeps it
```

The preregistration cell, copied into your notes, is your preregistration record.

## Task 5, continued – Fit, report and place {#task-5-fit-report}

This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part that your classmates cannot copy from you: together the class samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. `run_spec()` fits your declared specification and prints the same lines as `try_spec()`. It refuses to run if the preregistration cell has changed since `prereg()` read it.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
run_spec(my_spec)
```

The difference is in percentage points, and a value below zero means that replies to Hispanic names greeted the sender by name less often, the direction of the claim. Whether it is significant is decided by the test of the model, and the line headed `Verdict:` says which of the four cases your result falls in.

Now send it to the class chart. The submission is built from your declaration, so there is nothing to fill in or transcribe. The cell prints your submission line and the address of a pre-filled form; open the address in a new tab and press **Send**. Your mark joins the live [class chart]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) within seconds, this time as a filled circle labelled **declared**, carrying the same tag as your exploratory result. If you have reloaded this page since Task 4, the session has forgotten that tag, so pass it back with `report_result(nickname = "your-tag")`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
report_result()
```

If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator, who adds your mark to the chart.

Finally, place your result on the curve of the claim: the 64 specifications that the menu keeps, ranked from the most negative estimate, with yours ringed. The first cell reads and ranks the curve, and prints nothing.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
spec_curve <- utils::read.csv("data/spec_curve.csv") |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("b_pp") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rank = 1:n(),
                          emails = factor(population, levels = c("replies", "all"),
                                          labels = c("replies only", "all delivered emails")))
```

The second picks out your specification by the choices of the preregistration cell, again without printing anything.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Yours, chosen with dplyr, because datawizard cannot see the my_ choices of
# the preregistration cell
mine <- spec_curve |>
  dplyr::filter(comparison == my_comparison, population == my_population, uncoded == my_uncoded,
                model == my_model, adjust == my_adjust)
```

The third draws the curve and rings yours.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
tinyplot::tinytheme("minimal")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank | emails, data = spec_curve, pch = 16,
                   palette = c("#0e3b6a", "#2b8585"), legend = list("right!", title = "Emails counted"),
                   ylim = c(min(spec_curve$b_pp), 0),
                   xlab = "The 64 specifications, from the most negative estimate",
                   ylab = "Hispanic minus comparison names (points)")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank, data = spec_curve, type = tinyplot::type_hline(h = 0), col = "grey60", add = TRUE)
# your specification, ringed; clim keeps a single ring at the size of cex
tinyplot::tinyplot(b_pp ~ rank, data = mine, type = tinyplot::type_points(clim = c(3, 3)),
                   pch = 1, cex = 3, lwd = 2.5, col = "#8b1538", add = TRUE)
tinyplot::tinytheme()
```

All 64 estimates lie below zero, from −20.0 to −12.1 points, and every one of them is significant at 5% under the test of its model. The two clusters are the two answers to the decision on which emails are counted: counting every delivered email moves the estimate about 5 points towards zero, and no other decision moves it by more than about 2.7 points. Within these data the claim holds under every choice on the menu, and only its size moves. The [Class results]({{< var cases.housing.live-results-url >}}) page sets the class submissions beside this curve.

If you want a second declared specification, edit the preregistration cell, run it and the `prereg()` cell again, then rerun `run_spec(my_spec)`. The chart will still label it declared, so be clear with yourself about what the second one is. Your first declaration was made without knowing its result. Anything after it was not, which puts it back in the same category as Task 4, and you should say so wherever you write about the result.

## Taking it home

This page keeps nothing once you refresh it, so work you want to keep belongs in the downloadable workspace. Putting that work under version control and publishing the rendered report is the natural next step. The [Git and GitHub module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/git-github.html) of the companion curriculum explains it click by click.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## The downloadable workspace

The exercise on this page, Tasks 1 to 5, also exists in the downloadable workspace, the folder that you open in your IDE, edit and render offline, and keep after the session. The same folder holds the five reproductions of Task 3 as a script, and a GitHub Actions workflow that renders the report and publishes it to GitHub Pages once the folder is pushed to a GitHub repository whose Pages source is set to GitHub Actions. The folder is maintained in the [`ar4ds-housing-workspace`]({{< var cases.housing.template-repo >}}) repository, and it is yours to reuse.
